games.title: Phantasy Star
games.note: Heroine Alis leads a party through smooth 3D dungeons programmed by Yuji Naka.

games.title: Phantasy Star Online
games.note: Brought online co-op RPG play to consoles through the Dreamcast's built-in modem.

games.title: Monster Hunter
games.note: Built for online play on the PlayStation 2; its Japanese servers ran until 2011.

games.title: Resident Evil Outbreak
games.note: An online co-op Resident Evil for PlayStation 2, made in the same Capcom network push as Monster Hunter.

games.title: Monster Hunter Freedom Unite
games.note: Released in Japan as Monster Hunter Portable 2nd G, where local PSP hunting parties made it a hit.

games.title: Monster Hunter 4
games.note: Added climbing and mounting monsters; it reached the West as Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate.

games.title: Dauntless
games.note: Phoenix Labs was formed by former Riot Games developers.

games.title: Wild Hearts
games.note: Published by EA under its EA Originals label.

games.title: Tales of Phantasia
games.note: Its cartridge held a sung opening theme, rare on the Super Famicom.

games.title: Tales of Symphonia
games.note: The first main Tales game with 3D graphics.

games.title: Star Ocean
games.note: tri-Ace's debut, made by staff who left Wolf Team during Tales of Phantasia.

games.title: Valkyria Chronicles
games.note: Its CANVAS engine makes the 3D world look like moving watercolor sketches.

games.title: Sakura Wars
games.note: Mixes dating-sim conversations with mech battles in a steampunk version of 1920s Tokyo.

games.title: Skies of Arcadia
games.note: Sky pirates sail airships between floating islands.

games.title: Shenmue
games.note: Yu Suzuki's recreation of 1986 Yokosuka, with day-night cycles and weather; one of the most expensive games of its time.

games.title: SpikeOut
games.note: A networked arcade brawler from Toshihiro Nagoshi's team at Sega.

games.title: Yakuza
games.note: Crime novelist Hase Seishu helped edit its story, set in a fictional version of Tokyo's Kabukicho.

games.title: Yakuza 0
games.note: A 1988-set prequel that became many Western players' way into the series.

games.title: Yakuza: Like a Dragon
games.note: Its turn-based combat was first shown in an April Fools' Day trailer that many fans took as a joke.

games.title: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth
games.note: Takes the series to Hawaii.

games.title: Drakengard
games.note: Yoko Taro's directing debut; its strangest ending leads into Nier.

games.title: Nier
games.note: Released in Japan as two versions with different heroes, Replicant and Gestalt.

games.title: Nier: Automata
games.note: Yoko Taro's story of androids 2B and 9S unfolds across several playthroughs and endings.

games.title: Stellar Blade
games.note: Directed by Kim Hyung-tae, best known as an illustrator for Blade & Soul.

games.title: The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky
games.note: Begins a connected saga that runs across more than ten games.

games.title: Master of Orion
games.note: A preview describing it as 'eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate' gave the 4X genre its name.

games.title: Path of Exile
games.note: Made in Auckland and free to play, with a passive skill tree of more than 1,300 nodes.

games.title: Path of Exile 2
games.note: In early access since December 2024.

games.title: Torchlight
games.note: Runic Games was founded by Travis Baldree and Diablo co-creators Max and Erich Schaefer, with Peter Hu.

games.title: Fate
games.note: Its pet can carry loot back to town to sell, an idea Torchlight reused.

games.title: Hellgate: London
games.note: Flagship Studios closed within a year of its launch.

games.title: Titan Quest
games.note: Brian Sullivan conceived it while working on the Greek-themed Age of Empires.

games.title: Grim Dawn
games.note: Crowdfunded on Kickstarter by a small team of former Iron Lore developers.

games.title: Last Epoch
games.note: Kickstarted in 2018 and in early access from 2019 before its 2024 launch.

games.title: Dragon's Dogma
games.note: Players climb onto giant monsters and hire AI companions called pawns, which other players create.

links.took: First-person dungeon crawling, popularized by Wizardry among Japanese designers.
links.added: Smooth-scrolling 3D corridors, a science-fiction star system and a heroine, Alis.

src.t: Wikipedia: Phantasy Star ('Many Japanese game designers were inspired by Western RPGs such as Ultima and Wizardry')

links.extra: The source names Western RPGs as a general influence, not a direct claim.

links.took: The console RPG boom that Dragon Quest started on the Famicom.
links.added: Science-fiction planets, animated monsters and 3D dungeons on the Master System.
links.extra: The team was also strongly influenced by Star Wars.

links.took: The Phantasy Star name, its science-fiction setting and Rappy monsters.
links.added: Real-time online co-op for four players on the Dreamcast.

links.took: Loot-driven dungeon runs; Yuji Naka's team adopted Diablo as its main inspiration.
links.added: Four-player online co-op on a console, with lobbies and Mag companions.
links.extra: Naka also studied Ultima Online and EverQuest but chose not to make an MMO.

links.took: Teaming up online to take on stronger monsters in co-op missions.
links.added: Hunting huge creatures and crafting gear from their parts.

src.t: Wikipedia: Phantasy Star Online ('believed to be a major influence on Capcom's Monster Hunter series')

links.took: Resident Evil's zombies, Raccoon City and survival-horror play.
links.added: Online co-op for four players on PlayStation 2.

links.took: Capcom's online PS2 work; Ryozo Tsujimoto called Monster Hunter its culmination.
links.added: Co-op hunts of giant creatures instead of zombie survival.
links.extra: Tsujimoto named Outbreak and the racing game Auto Modellista as the two earlier network titles.

links.took: Hunting quests, monster parts and weapon crafting.
links.added: Handheld local co-op, Felyne cat companions and many more monsters.

links.took: The hunt, carve and craft loop of the portable games.
links.added: Vertical maps, climbing and mounting monsters, and the Insect Glaive.

links.took: Directors Kaname Fujioka and Yuya Tokuda and the series' core hunting loop.
links.added: Seamless maps without loading zones and a push for Western players.

links.took: Co-op hunts against large monsters and gear crafted from their parts.
links.added: Free-to-play, cross-platform hunting on floating islands.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dauntless ('heavily inspired by, as well as frequently compared to, Capcom's Monster Hunter series')

links.took: Big co-op monster hunts and crafting from monster parts.
links.added: Karakuri: instantly building springs, walls and traps in the middle of a fight.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wild Hearts (citing The Verge and GamesRadar+)

links.extra: The Verge called it 'a fresh take on Monster Hunter with a dash of Fortnite'.

links.took: Building structures instantly in the middle of combat.
links.added: Karakuri contraptions used against giant beasts fused with nature.

links.took: Real-time fighting game controls, which were popular at the time.
links.added: The Linear Motion Battle System: RPG heroes fighting in real time on a 2D line.

src.t: Wikipedia: Tales of Phantasia (battle system 'inspired by fighting games')

links.extra: The source credits fighting games in general, not Street Fighter II by name.

links.took: Staff who left Wolf Team to found tri-Ace, and a similar real-time battle system.
links.added: A science-fiction frame, private actions in towns and item creation.

links.took: Real-time Linear Motion battles and the series' fantasy adventure style.
links.added: 3D battlefields, cel-shaded characters and two worlds bound together.

links.took: Real-time Tales combat and a story of two linked worlds.
links.added: Painterly Unreal Engine visuals and Boost Strikes with party members.

links.took: Creators Ryutaro Nonaka and Shuntaro Tanaka and its mix of tactics and drama.
links.added: BLiTZ: turn-based command with real-time third-person movement.
links.extra: The creators said similarities came from shared teams and gameplay styles.

links.took: Shuntaro Tanaka, who was finishing its GameCube port, and its art direction.
links.added: A watercolor-style CANVAS engine and a European-style war setting.

links.took: A detailed modern Japanese city full of side activities and stories.
links.added: Brutal brawling and a crime drama in Kamurocho, a Tokyo red-light district.
links.extra: Newtype USA called it 'the adult-themed spiritual successor' to Shenmue.

links.took: Toshihiro Nagoshi's earlier brawler, used as the basis for combat.
links.added: Story-driven street fights in a living city full of minigames.

links.took: Kazuma Kiryu, Kamurocho brawling and side stories.
links.added: A 1988 bubble-era setting and a second hero, Goro Majima.

links.took: City exploration, substories and minigames.
links.added: A new hero, Ichiban Kasuga, and turn-based party combat in Yokohama.

links.took: Ichiban's turn-based party combat and job system.
links.added: A trip to Hawaii and Kazuma Kiryu as a second lead.

links.took: Turn-based party battles, framed by hero Ichiban Kasuga's love of Dragon Quest.
links.added: Street fights in modern Yokohama where Ichiban imagines enemies as RPG monsters.

src.t: GamerMatters, the game's lead writer on the switch to turn-based play

links.extra: Yuji Horii gave Sega permission to name Dragon Quest in the game.

links.took: Its fifth ending, which leaves a ruined Earth.
links.added: A new hero, bullet-hell magic and shifts between game genres.

links.took: Combat and action inspired by the God of War series.
links.added: Genre shifts into top-down, side-scrolling and text-adventure sections.
links.extra: The source cites the God of War series generally.

links.took: Yoko Taro's world, melancholy story and multiple endings.
links.added: PlatinumGames' fast action combat and the androids 2B and 9S.

links.took: PlatinumGames' action design, the reason Square Enix chose the studio.
links.added: An open world, RPG systems and switches to shoot 'em up views.

src.t: Wikipedia: Nier: Automata ('high-quality action games such as Bayonetta')

links.took: Open-world RPG design, which partly inspired PlatinumGames' staff.
links.added: Fast character-action combat inside a ruined open world.

links.took: Stylish android combat; Kim Hyung-tae called Nier: Automata a huge driving force.
links.added: Parry-focused duels on a post-apocalyptic Earth retaken from the Naytiba.
links.extra: Yoko Taro later praised Stellar Blade, and the games shared a crossover DLC.

links.took: Parry-based duels against tough bosses.
links.added: A sci-fi heroine, combo chains and Beta skills.

links.took: Flashy combos and a stylish heroine.
links.added: Perfect parries and dodges in a semi-open world.

links.took: miHoYo's anime-style action and character-collecting gacha model.
links.added: An open world of seven nations with elemental reaction combat.

links.took: Alternate versions of Honkai characters and the series' universe.
links.added: Turn-based combat aboard an interstellar train.

src.t: Wikipedia: Honkai: Star Rail ('the spiritual successor to Honkai Impact 3rd')

links.took: Exploration, dungeons and the gacha system carried over from Genshin Impact.
links.added: Turn-based battles built around breaking enemy weaknesses.

links.took: Turn-based combat style; the development team cited Persona 5 as inspiration.
links.added: A free-to-play space adventure with collectible characters.

links.took: Turn-based battle design; the team cited the Trails series as inspiration.
links.added: Mobile-first design and a space opera setting.
links.extra: The source names the Trails series; Trails in the Sky is its first game.

links.took: Falcom's The Legend of Heroes line, which began as a Dragon Slayer entry.
links.added: Turn-based grid battles and a long, connected story.
links.extra: The Legend of Heroes started as Dragon Slayer VI in 1989.

links.took: Tech-tree progression, which David Brevik turned into character skill trees.
links.added: Skill trees for five classes in a real-time action RPG.

links.took: Research-tree progression, named alongside Civilization as a source of skill trees.
links.added: Point-by-point skill investment for each hero.

links.took: Online play features that Brevik studied and tried to improve on.
links.added: Battle.net co-op, trading and closed realms for characters.
links.extra: Wikipedia ties part of the game's delay to this focus.

links.took: Dark gothic tone, loot hunting and isometric action, borrowed heavily.
links.added: Socketed skill gems, a huge passive tree and a free-to-play model.

src.t: Wikipedia: Path of Exile ('borrows heavily from the Diablo series, particularly Diablo II')

links.took: The Materia system, the model for slotting skill gems into gear sockets.
links.added: Linked sockets that combine active skills with support gems.
links.extra: The team also named Magic: The Gathering among its inspirations.

links.took: Skill gems, the passive tree and the world of Wraeclast.
links.added: Slower, dodge-based combat and a new campaign.

links.took: The isometric loot-and-skills formula that Diablo II popularized.
links.added: Time travel between eras and a skill tree for every individual skill.
links.extra: Genre lineage only; no developer statement was checked.

links.took: Blizzard North co-founders Max and Erich Schaefer and their click-to-loot formula.
links.added: A bright cartoon style, a pet that sells loot, and fishing.

src.t: PC Gamer, 'Light from the Darkness: The Making of Torchlight'

links.took: Travis Baldree's compact dungeon crawler with a pet that sells loot in town.
links.added: Bigger production values, three classes and a modding toolkit.

links.took: Isometric dungeon looting; Travis Baldree set out to combine Diablo and NetHack.
links.added: A single small town, a pet companion and casual-friendly pacing.
links.extra: GameSpot also noted its strong resemblance to Diablo.

links.took: Roguelike depth that Baldree wanted to mix with Diablo's action.
links.added: Real-time combat and a pet that fights beside you.

links.took: Runic's bright loot-driven action and pets.
links.added: Online co-op and an open overworld.

links.took: Leadership from former Blizzard North executives who oversaw Diablo.
links.added: A first- or third-person demon apocalypse in a ruined London.
links.extra: Flagship Studios was founded by Bill Roper, Max and Erich Schaefer and David Brevik.

links.took: Click-to-fight dungeon looting, prompting constant comparisons to Diablo.
links.added: Greek, Egyptian and Asian myth and a dual-mastery class system.

links.took: Brian Sullivan's Greek setting idea, which came while he worked on Age of Empires.
links.added: A mythological action RPG instead of a strategy game.

links.took: The licensed Titan Quest engine and systems, built on by former Iron Lore staff.
links.added: A grim gaslamp-fantasy setting, factions and constellation devotions.

links.took: Diablo II's darkness, which the art team paired with Diablo III's hand-painted feel.
links.added: A seamless open world shared with other players.

links.took: A large open fantasy world, one of the Western RPGs Capcom aimed to emulate.
links.added: Climbing giant monsters and AI pawns made by other players.
links.extra: Fable II is also named; Itsuno later compared his goal to Skyrim.

links.took: Western open-world RPG freedom that the developers wanted to match.
links.added: Physical combat with grabbing and climbing on enemies.

links.took: Action combat ideas from Devil May Cry, which staff drew on.
links.added: Class vocations and grappling onto monsters in an open world.
links.extra: Director Hideaki Itsuno had directed Devil May Cry sequels.

links.took: Pawns, vocations and climbing on huge monsters.
links.added: A denser open world and new vocations such as the Trickster.

updates.value: Began as Condor's turn-based roguelike pitch; Blizzard asked for real-time play, which David Brevik then built.
The first Monster Hunter released worldwide on the same day; it became Capcom's best-selling game at the time.
